uk-mortgage-calculator.assumptionNote: This uses standard monthly amortisation at a fixed interest rate. It excludes arrangement fees, valuation fees, stamp duty, and insurance. UK mortgages are often fixed for 2-5 years then revert to a variable rate.

faqs.a: Loan-to-value (LTV) is your loan as a percentage of the property price. A £200,000 loan on a £250,000 home is 80% LTV. Lower LTV almost always means a better interest rate, because the lender's risk is smaller.

Overpayments cut the loan balance, so you pay less interest overall and finish earlier. Most UK fixed deals let you overpay up to 10% of the balance per year without an early repayment charge. Even £50 a month extra makes a noticeable difference over 25 years.

They are loans against the home's equity for over-55s, with no monthly repayments - interest rolls up and is repaid when you sell, move into care, or die. They are heavily regulated in the UK and require independent advice. They are very different from standard repayment mortgages.

UK stamp duty on a £250,000 home is £0 for a first-time buyer (relief up to £425,000), or £2,500 for an existing homeowner (£0 on the first £125,000, then 2% on the next £125,000). Rates change, so always check the latest HMRC thresholds before budgeting.
faqs.q: How much stamp duty will I pay?

faqs.a: The mortgage term is how long you take to repay. A longer term means lower monthly payments but much more total interest. A 30-year term on £200,000 at 4.5% costs about £35,000 more in interest than a 25-year term. Choose the shortest term whose payments you can comfortably afford.
faqs.q: 25 or 30 year term - which is better?

faqs.a: Most first-time buyers put down 5-10%. A bigger deposit unlocks lower LTV bands and cheaper rates: moving from 95% to 90% LTV usually cuts the rate noticeably. Below 60% LTV you get the market's best deals, but tying up all your savings leaves no emergency fund.

uk-mortgage-calculator.formula:
Monthly rate r = annual rate / 12.
Number of payments n = years x 12.
Monthly payment = P x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n).
Total payable = monthly payment x n.
Total interest = total payable - loan amount.
howTo: Enter the property price and your deposit.
Enter the annual interest rate (the initial fixed rate from your offer or comparison).
Choose the mortgage term in years.
Read your monthly payment, LTV, total interest, and total payable.
Try different deposits and terms to see which combination fits your budget.
keyFacts: UK mortgages are usually repayment mortgages: each payment covers interest plus part of the capital.
Most deals are fixed for 2-5 years, then move to the lender's standard variable rate.
A bigger deposit means a lower loan-to-value and usually a cheaper interest rate.
First-time buyers in the UK can often buy with a 5% deposit.
Monthly payments must pass lender affordability stress tests, not just the headline rate.
Early repayment charges apply if you leave a fixed deal early - typically 1-5% of the balance.
